vignette: Nadia, a 59-year-old Middle Eastern woman and police officer, has been haunted by the assault she experienced six months ago. She was on patrol when an intruder attacked her in a dark alley, leaving her shaken and physically injured. Since then, the event has left a profound mark on Nadia’s daily life. Her heart racing is often triggered by driving with others, reminding her of the fear she felt during the assault. The sound of approaching cars or sirens can make her pulse quicken, signaling danger even in safe settings. This somatic trigger has led her to isolate completely from friends and family. She fears that driving with others could reawaken the same terror she experienced when the intruder attacked. Nadia’s hypervigilance extends beyond driving; she is constantly vigilant for dangerous people, which makes social interactions overwhelming. Her thoughts are consumed by a constant monitoring of her own mind, worried about going crazy. This hyper-awareness has made it nearly impossible to maintain normal relationships or engage in activities that once brought her joy. When Nadia recalls the assault, her memories are vivid and auditory, often replaying sounds from the event as if they were happening in real time. The clarity of these memories brings back the same terror she felt at the time. She has come to believe that her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger, even when she is safe at home or work. This belief exacerbates her isolation and hypervigilance. Nadia feels deeply betrayed by what happened to her; she perceives it as deeply unfair and unjust. The lack of justice surrounding the assault has reinforced her sense that she cannot rely on others for support. This negative appraisal further fuels her tendency to isolate herself completely, cutting off all contact with friends and family. Her hypervigilance extends into every aspect of her life, making everyday activities like driving or socializing feel fraught with danger. She often hears sounds from the assault in her head when she is alone, which triggers vivid memories that bring back the same terror. These auditory recollections make it hard for Nadia to relax and trust others around her. Over time, this cycle has worsened. Her constant fear of violence and reliance on hypervigilance have made her increasingly isolated. She avoids driving with anyone and cuts off all social contact, believing that these actions are necessary to stay safe. This isolation only deepens her negative appraisals about the unfairness of what happened and her distrust in others. Nadia’s work as a police officer has also been affected by her symptoms. Her hypervigilance makes it difficult for her to engage with colleagues, leading to strained relationships at work. She fears that driving on patrol could trigger memories of the assault, making her less effective in her duties and causing tension among her team. What frightens Nadia most is the continuous cycle of fear and isolation she feels trapped within. Her sense of injustice and lack of trust in others has left her feeling alone and vulnerable. Finally, after months of struggling silently, Nadia decided to seek help because she realized that this cycle was affecting every aspect of her life—both personally and professionally. She is most hopeful for a return to the sense of safety and trust she once had, hoping therapy can help break this vicious cycle and restore some normalcy in her daily life.
